vignette:
Here is a clinical vignette written from the perspective of a psychologist.

---

**Patient: Mr. A. (Age 75, Middle Eastern, Widowed, Sculptor)**

Mr. A. is a man who seems to have been carved from the same stone he works with. He is solid, quiet, and when he speaks, his words feel measured, as if he is chipping away at a block of silence to find the right shape. He came to my office at the insistence of his daughter, who, he admits with a sigh, is worried about him. He is not worried. He is simply… tired.

He tells me the story of the accident slowly, his hands resting on his knees, palms up. Ten months ago, he was in his studio—a converted garage filled with the fine, white dust of alabaster. He was working on a large piece, a figure of a woman reclining. He needed to move the block, so he used a hydraulic lift, a machine he had operated a thousand times. But this time, the chain snapped. The half-ton block of stone swung free, catching him across the chest and pinning him to the concrete floor.

He does not describe the pain. He describes the sound. “It was a wet crack,” he says, looking past me. “Like a tree branch, but inside me. I knew I was broken.” He lay there for two hours before a neighbor heard his shouts. He remembers the cold of the floor against his cheek, the taste of stone dust in his mouth, and the absolute certainty that he was going to die alone, pinned under his own creation.

Physically, he healed. Three cracked ribs, a fractured pelvis. The doctors called him lucky. But Mr. A. does not feel lucky. He feels hollowed out.

Since the accident, he has not entered his studio. The key hangs on a hook by the back door. He walks past it every morning to get his mail. He touches the key, but he cannot turn it. The thought of the smell of the dust, the hum of the ventilation fan, the sight of that unfinished figure—it sends a wave of heat up his chest and makes his vision blur. He has tried to force himself, standing at the threshold for ten minutes at a time, but his legs will not obey. He tells me it is not fear, exactly. It is a certainty that if he goes in, the ceiling will fall, or the floor will give way, or the air itself will turn solid and crush him again.

He used to work with his hands from dawn until dusk. Now, his hands twitch in his lap, tracing the shape of absent tools. He has tried to whittle a piece of driftwood he found on a walk, but after five minutes, his heart began to pound so hard he thought he was having a heart attack. He stopped. He has stopped many things.

Sleep is a battlefield. He lies in the bed he shared with his wife, who died six years ago, and listens to the house settle. The creak of a pipe is the groan of the lift. The hum of the refrigerator is the chain pulling taut. He will jolt awake, convinced he feels the weight on his chest, the grit of the floor on his cheek. He now sleeps in a chair in the living room, the lights on, the television murmuring to no one.

He is irritable with his daughter. He snaps at her when she calls, then feels a deep, cold shame. He has stopped seeing his old friends from the art community. They mean well, but their talk of new projects and exhibitions feels like a language he has forgotten. He feels separate, behind a pane of thick glass. He watches the world move, but he cannot feel its rhythm.

When I ask him what he misses most, he does not say sculpting. He says, “I miss the quiet in my head. Before, when I worked, there was only the stone and me. Now, there is only the noise of it falling.” He looks down at his hands, still and empty. “I am a sculptor,” he says, not to me, but to the floor. “But I have nothing left to hold.”
